chapters.title: Chapter 6: Evaluating a Market Making Business

lessons.title: Case Study: Telling a Genuine Edge From a Lucky Quarter

body.text: A quarter of excellent numbers proves a desk had a good quarter. It does not prove the desk has a genuine edge, because a genuine edge is only visible once it has actually been tested, and a calm quarter never tests anything.

children.text: A market maker runs the same book, on the same instrument, with the same underlying pricing model, across two consecutive quarters. Q1 is unusually calm: 60 sessions with no significant volatility events. Q2 runs into three genuine volatility episodes, each resembling the kind of one-sided flow covered in Chapter 3's case study. Every metric from this chapter's earlier lessons is available for both quarters.

body.caption: The same desk's metrics, calm quarter vs volatile quarter

children.text: Judged on Q1 alone, this looks like an outstanding market making business: high spread capture, a strong Sharpe ratio, and a small drawdown. Q2 shows every metric moving in the direction Chapter 6 warned about. Spread capture rate falling while fill ratio rises simultaneously is exactly the low-capture, high-fill quadrant from this chapter's first lesson, consistent with facing more informed, harder-to-price order flow. Holding time more than quadrupling, from Little's Law in the second lesson, shows positions sitting exposed far longer during the volatile stretches. Sharpe ratio collapsing and maximum drawdown ballooning to more than seven times its Q1 level are exactly the kind of gap the third lesson's Book A versus Book B comparison was built to anticipate.

body.text: None of these Q2 numbers are, on their own, surprising. A market making book that never sees its metrics move during a genuinely volatile stretch should be more suspicious, not less, since it would suggest the book was never actually exposed to real risk in the first place.

children.text: So Was Q1 Skill or Luck?

The honest answer is that Q1's numbers alone could never distinguish a genuinely well-priced quoting model from one that simply had not yet been tested, since a calm quarter cannot reveal how a desk behaves under stress. Q2 is what actually answers the question, and the answer here is a genuine, if imperfect, edge rather than pure luck: spread capture rate fell hard but stayed positive at 55%, meaning the desk was still converting more than half its theoretical spread into real profit even while facing meaningfully tougher order flow, and Sharpe ratio, while far lower, stayed positive rather than turning negative. A desk with no real edge behind its Q1 numbers would more plausibly have shown spread capture collapsing toward zero or negative, and a Q2 Sharpe ratio well below zero, in a genuinely volatile quarter.

That said, resilience is not the same as good enough. A maximum drawdown of ₹640,000 in a single quarter, more than seven times the calm quarter's figure, is a legitimate signal that risk management, position sizing, and how early the desk escalates from skewing to an aggressive unwind, deserves real scrutiny, even though the core pricing model itself appears to have a genuine edge underneath the rough quarter.

body.title: A Newer Desk's Suspiciously Perfect Numbers
body.scenario: A newer market making desk reports a spread capture rate of 92%, a Sharpe ratio of 3.8, and a maximum drawdown of only ₹12,000, all over its first two quarters of operation. Its fill ratio and holding time both look excellent by this chapter's standards throughout.
body.prompt: Using the framework from this lesson, how much confidence should an investor place in these numbers as evidence of a genuine, durable edge?
body.modelAnswer: Very little confidence should be placed in these numbers as proof of a durable edge, precisely because the case study in this lesson shows that calm-period metrics cannot distinguish skill from luck. If this newer desk's two quarters have not yet included a genuinely volatile, high-adverse-selection stretch comparable to Q2 in this lesson's case study, its excellent numbers may simply reflect a pricing model that has not yet been tested, rather than one that has been tested and held up. The appropriate response is not to dismiss the desk, but to treat its numbers as unproven until they have survived a real stress period, and to watch specifically how spread capture rate, fill ratio, and drawdown behave the first time one occurs.

body.title: What Would Actually Worry an Investor
body.question: Building on this lesson's case study, which outcome in a volatile quarter would most concern an investor about whether a desk's edge is genuine?
options: Spread capture rate falling from 85% to 55%, while staying positive
Spread capture rate collapsing to near 0% and Sharpe ratio turning clearly negative
body.explanation: A drop in spread capture rate, a rise in fill ratio, and a larger drawdown are all expected, even healthy, signs that a volatile quarter genuinely tested the book, exactly as this lesson's case study showed. Spread capture rate collapsing to near zero alongside a clearly negative Sharpe ratio would suggest something different: that the pricing model was not actually earning a real edge once tested, which is a far more serious concern than metrics simply looking worse than a calm quarter.

points: A calm quarter's strong metrics cannot distinguish a genuinely well-priced market making model from one that has simply never been tested
A volatile quarter is what actually reveals whether a desk's edge is real, by showing how spread capture rate, fill ratio, holding time, Sharpe ratio, and drawdown behave under stress
Metrics worsening in a volatile quarter, lower spread capture, higher fill ratio, longer holding time, lower Sharpe, larger drawdown, is expected and does not by itself disprove a genuine edge

A spread capture rate and Sharpe ratio that stay positive, even if much lower, under real stress is meaningfully different from both collapsing toward zero or negative, which would suggest the earlier good numbers were mostly luck

Resilience under stress and good risk management are separate questions; a desk can have a genuine underlying edge and still show unacceptably large drawdowns that demand better position sizing and escalation discipline

This closes Chapter 6's arc: spread capture rate and fill ratio evaluate the core quoting mechanism, holding time and turnover evaluate duration risk, and Sharpe and drawdown evaluate the resulting P&L, with all five only becoming genuinely informative once read together across both calm and volatile conditions
